Every now and then, you need to find an export manager.

And then you start talking to the hiring manager. What they actually need is someone who will find new markets, research competitors, identify potential customers, build a distributor network, negotiate contracts, manage logistics, coordinate marketing, attend trade fairs, speak several languages and, naturally, bring in revenue...

Congratulations. You've just been asked to recruit an entire international business development department in one person. 😊 Some of the myriad qualities include:

1. Curiosity: They don't just want to know who might buy the product, but WHY someone would buy it over there.

2. Research skills: Finding a country on a map is easy. Understanding its business environment is something else. Only this far will #AI help.

3. Cultural intelligence. Doing business in Germany, Kazakhstan, Spain or Denmark requires different approaches. Also, local language may be a must, or not.

4. Relationship building: International business often runs on trust. A good export manager knows how to build relationships with distributors, agents, partners and customers, sometimes long before the first deal happens.

5. Sales skills: Let's not forget the obvious. At some point, all that research, networking and market development needs to translate into revenue.

6. Financial literacy: Revenue isn't the same as profitability. Margins, logistics, Incoterms, payment terms, and currency risks matter. Also, sales cycles of anything longer than 6 months burn cash.

7. Independence and resourcefulness: Especially in smaller companies, there won't always be a marketing manager, a local rep, or a manager with instructions at hand. A good export manager knows how to get things moving, find solutions and bring in expertise when needed.

8. Strategic patience: Getting out there takes time. Sometimes months, likely - years. A good export manager needs to balance short-term sales targets with longer-term market development. As does the hiring manager.

Now, one more thing. Before writing that job description, I'd suggest answering a fairly simple question: Who are you looking for?  
A Hunter, someone who opens doors and closes deals?
A Market Builder, someone who establishes your presence, develops partnerships and creates new opportunities?
An Export Director, someone who coordinates the entire international operation?

These are three rather different profiles. You might find someone who combines all three, but don't be surprised if they come with a slightly different salary expectation. After all, you're not just hiring someone to sell abroad. You're trusting them to represent your business in markets where your company might have little or no presence.

And that's quite a responsibility. Ping me for more personal advice.

The AI layoff that starts as an outsourcing contract.

Qantas told staff on Tuesday that about 850 corporate roles will be affected over the coming years, starting with finance, procurement, HR and marketing by mid-2027.

The reason given is technology and AI. The mechanism is Accenture. The work moves to Accenture's team, mostly in India. Automation and AI come later, inside Accenture's operation.

Qantas has a fair case. More than 1,000 legacy applications that were never built to work together is a real cost, and the airline is still hiring pilots, engineers and staff for a 400-role tech hub in Adelaide.

The order still matters. Outsource first and automate second, and when AI eventually shrinks those roles, the cuts land in a vendor's headcount. Qantas never has to announce them.

In August, the union said Qantas had told it there was “no plan to offshore any Australian jobs.”

If your company signs a “transformation partnership” with a consultancy, read which functions move first. That list is the automation roadmap.

Most AI job losses at big companies will arrive this way, as an outsourcing line one year and a smaller contract renewal a few years later.

Should your next AI hire be a contractor?

The test is whether the work has an end date, and whether anyone needs to own it once that date passes.

If you’re moving a model from pilot into production, integrating a system, or clearing a backlog someone scoped months ago, a contractor fits. 

They come in on a day rate for a fixed term, start in weeks rather than months, and compliance and payroll sit with whoever placed them. If the work runs longer than planned, the extension gets managed rather than becoming a new search.

If the thing you’re building has to keep running after that first delivery, and somebody has to answer for it when it misbehaves at 2am, you’re hiring permanently, through contingent or retained search depending on how scarce the skills are.

Three things decide whether the contract route works, and all of them come before the job spec.

- Decide what finished looks like first, not a date in a plan but the state the work has to be in for the contract to close.
- Have the person who inherits the work in post and involved before the contract ends, because a handover arranged in the final fortnight rarely survives the first incident.
- Treat a third extension as a signal, because by that point the work has become a permanent role and renewing is usually the more expensive way to fill it.

For anyone hiring in the UK, this is a live market. Demand for temporary tech staff hit its highest level since January 2023 in September, growing for three months straight, with AI a large part of it.

Send us what you’re hiring for at hello@ralyd.ai and we’ll tell you whether contract, contingent or retained search suits the work.

The EU AI Act delay isn't a reprieve for HR. 
Some of it already applies to you:

The high-risk deadline for hiring and people AI has moved to December 2027.
Yet only 18% of European employers say they're very prepared (Littler, 2025). Many HR teams heard "delay" and stopped reading.

Here's what the delay doesn't change:

1️⃣ Emotion recognition at work is already banned 
↳ That ban has applied since February 2025, with fines up to €35m or 7% of global turnover (EU AI Act, Articles 5 and 99).

2️⃣ AI literacy is still your job 
↳ The Digital Omnibus softened the rule, but employers must still take steps to build AI literacy in staff who use AI (Regulation (EU) 2026/1744).

3️⃣ Hiring and people decisions are high-risk 
↳ CV screening, promotion, dismissal and performance monitoring all sit on the high-risk list (EU AI Act, Annex III).

4️⃣ Your vendor's compliance isn't yours 
↳ As the employer, you must assign oversight to people with the training and authority to override the tool (EU AI Act, Article 26).

5️⃣ Your people hear first 
↳ Workers and their representatives must be told BEFORE high-risk AI goes live at work (EU AI Act, Article 26).

But compliance is only the floor.
Look at that list again. 

Human oversight. Telling people before you act. Keeping a record of decisions.

None of that is new to good HR. 
The Act simply turns trust into an audit trail.

AI can screen a stack of CVs before lunch. 
It can't explain a rejection to the candidate. 
It can't decide what fair looks like in your organisation.

That judgement stays with you, with or without a regulation.

Save this post if you're reviewing HR tech contracts before 2027.

Which AI tool in your HR stack would you struggle to explain to your works council today? Drop a comment below.

Pendant ce temps, Anthropic vient de racheter Mithril Medicine, une biotech américaine qui n’avait qu’un seul salarié. Son fondateur a amené un traitement potentiel jusqu’aux premiers résultats chez la souris en moins de 18 mois, avec 8 consultants à temps partiel, 11 laboratoires externes et Claude pour orchestrer les contrats, la logistique et les expériences.

En France, j’ai l’impression que les biotechs prennent un train de retard, parce qu’elles pensent que l’IA, ce n’est pas encore pour elles.

Oui, la paillasse reste manuelle. Cependant, tout ce qui l’entoure ne l’est pas : la traçabilité du cahier de labo, l’analyse des données, la qualité, les commandes, le recrutement, les dossiers de financement et réglementaires, le reporting. C’est là que part une énorme partie du temps d’une biotech  ⌛  Il est temps de prendre le pli et d’agentiser tout le reste de la structure, voire la structure elle-même.

Je suis sans doute un peu biaisée puisque je partage mon quotidien avec quelqu’un qui ne me parle que d’agents IA, Antoine Sauvage a réussi à agentiser jusqu’à la charge mentale de notre foyer, deux enfants compris.

Alors chez Nūmi, on s’y est mis, toute l'équipe s'y est mise. Chaque semaine, je vous partagerai un skill développé par l’équipe, du simple remplissage du cahier de labo aux commandes, en passant par les plans d’expérience. Je partagerai également la structure qu’on a choisie pour partager ces skills en équipe sans dépendre d’un seul modèle d’IA  🔥 

-- 
"We're not allowed to use AI here."
"Biotech is bench work, you can't automate it." 🥼

These are two sentences I hear a lot these days, in job interviews and among biotech founders, and I find it crazy 🤯

Meanwhile, Anthropic has just acquired Mithril Medicine, a US biotech with a single employee. Its founder took a potential treatment to first results in mice in under 18 months, with 8 part-time consultants, 11 external labs and Claude orchestrating contracts, logistics and experiments.

In France, I feel biotechs are missing the train, because they think AI isn't for them.
Yes, bench work stays manual. But everything around it doesn't: lab notebook traceability, data analysis, quality, purchasing, hiring, funding and regulatory filings, reporting. That's where a huge share of a biotech's time goes ⌛ It's time to make the shift and run the rest of the company with agents.

So at Nūmi, we went for it, and the whole team is on board. Every week, I'll share a skill built by the team, from simply filling in the lab notebook to purchasing and experimental design. I'll also show the structure we chose to share these skills.

AI is about 10% of Infosys's revenue. The whole company grew 1.5% on last year.
 
Infosys says its AI work is growing fast.
 
So where did the growth go?
 
Its own outlook for the second half answers it. It names "continued sharing of AI driven productivity benefits" as a hit to second-half margins.
 
Clients ask for the AI saving to be passed on. To me, that means the price falls before the vendor keeps any of it.
 
So my view is simple. Selling AI does not pay if the client expects the same work cheaper.
 
The hour AI saves is repriced before the vendor can keep it.
 
Three things I would look at if I ran a delivery business:
 
1. The saving is priced in. Management says clients ask for productivity benefits to be passed on, and a small number go beyond Infosys's return thresholds. I would expect such terms to be hard to take back.
 
2. The cost side does not shrink on its own. Net headcount rose by about 4,400 in the quarter. Part of that is planned fresher hiring, but the people doing the work did not get cheaper.
 
3. Nobody outside can audit the AI label. Infosys does not publish the base behind its AI revenue, and says it is new work. One analyst says AI at about 10% of revenue is "not reflected in higher growth or margins or revenue per employee".
 
On any platform team, a saved hour behaves the same way.
 
Who owns it?
 
If nobody decides, the next request on the queue takes it.
 
On Monday, price the hour AI saves in your next proposal. The client already has.
 
One limit: Infosys says older contracts take a one-time price cut and the AI work is new revenue, so I cannot show from outside that the AI share is relabelled old work. I can only see that the total did not move.

Beyond the Chatbox:
​
OpenAI is changing the rules. I'm adapting before they do.
​
Starting in December, OpenAI says ChatGPT and Codex will move to a shared, token-based usage allowance for Plus, Pro and Business. Regular Instant chat won't draw from that shared allowance.
​
That made me reconsider a question I've been exploring for a while:
​
What if the productivity advantage isn't always choosing the most powerful reasoning mode – but building a better workflow around the AI you use every day?
​
I'm learning to do that now, before the transition.
​
Clearer task contracts. Longer work cycles. Explicit testing and self-review. Durable project context. A process that doesn't stop at the first confident "done."
​
One practical experiment is EPOCHBORN, a VR game project supported by four recurring Instant agents: game development, 3D asset creation, independent review and orchestration. I use a higher-reasoning chat when I need broader architectural thinking, strategic direction or deeper Game Bible work.
​
It's not hands-free magic. Instructions get misread. Integrations break. Reviews uncover real problems. But the project keeps progressing without me micromanaging every individual task.
​
And to be precise: OpenAI's statement about regular Instant chat does NOT mean scheduled agent tasks are necessarily unlimited or exempt from usage limits. The new system hasn't been fully rolled out yet.
​
My takeaway so far: the system around a model can be just as important as the model itself.
​
What are you changing in your AI workflows before December?
​

Is the Swiss recruitment market finally turning a corner?

Two reports make for interesting reading and suggest that hiring sentiment in Switzerland may be starting to shift.

The latest Swiss Staffingindex (Q3 2026) shows encouraging signs of stabilisation in permanent recruitment. While permanent placement revenue was still down 5.5% year-on-year, the improvement over the quarter is noteworthy: the decline narrowed from 9.3% in July to just 2.3% in September. Meanwhile, temporary employment grew by 3.9%.

Adding another interesting perspective, earlier Robert Half's Swiss research, based on a survey of 250 hiring managers, found that 38% plan to increase permanent headcount before the end of 2026. Within Technology and IT, the figures are equally encouraging, with 38% planning to increase permanent hiring, 27% contract hiring and 37% project-based hiring.

So, what does this tell us?
I believe we are seeing a gradual shift from hiring cautiously to hiring more strategically.

A few trends stand out to me:
• Technology and digital transformation: Investments in AI, cybersecurity, cloud infrastructure and digitalisation continue to create demand for specialised skills.
• Quality over quantity: Companies are becoming more deliberate about hiring, placing greater emphasis on the right expertise, adaptability and the ability to contribute to long-term business objectives.
• The changing nature of talent: Technical knowledge alone is no longer enough. Critical thinking, communication, commercial understanding and the ability to adapt are becoming equally important.
• A more strategic recruitment partnership: In a selective hiring environment, understanding a business's needs, identifying talent beyond the obvious candidate pool and building meaningful relationships become even more valuable.

While it may be too early to call this a full recovery, the direction is certainly encouraging.

My takeaway is that the next phase of recruitment will not simply be about filling vacancies. It will be about connecting businesses with the people who can help shape their future.

The market may be picking up, but the real opportunity lies in hiring smarter.

GTM leadership will change more in the next two years than in the last ten.

AI has made building cheap and easier than ever. Coding agents and vibe coding makes copying features easy.

Selling will become a scare skill and the most valuable skill in the next decade. 
Earning trust. Proving you're not bluffing is the thing software and AI can't do. (Yet). 

At my last roundtable, the commercial leaders and CROs running GTM in the room were all hiring more salespeople, not fewer.

They tell me, as more businesses use AI to build their own tools, customers think they can build the tools they used to pay for on their own. But buyers typically don’t see the implications and limitations of doing that, the security, the data, the upkeep Ect. 

So the skill set of the commercial person is more important now:

1/ Help buyers see around corners.
2/ Show them what companies like theirs are actually doing.
3/ Put them in contact with peers facing the same decisions/challenges. 

Will agents ever buy for us? Will they replace salespeople? For small purchases, yes. I can see a world where we will give an agent a credit card, a limit and some rules, and it'll buy.

But

For the big purchases, no. Buyers will still want to judge the vendor, share the decision with peers, build the business case and see an adoption plan.

There are so many soft skills that buyers will still want to assess before making a purchase.

Nobody wants to tell their board an AI agent signed the contract!

If anyone can build anything, I think the winners will be the people who can sell it.

Sarvam AI has hired the former head of Google Cloud India.
The headline adds his big-name past.
It skips what a hire like this can and cannot prove.

Myth: a famous hire means a startup is winning.
Reality: it often shows where the startup thinks it is stuck.

Sarvam named Sashikumar Sreedharan President and Chief Business Officer on Monday.
He will run its business across enterprises and government, per the announcement.
Marketing, finance and delivery also sit under him.

The company also signaled it needs an organization built for much bigger scale.
My read: companies hire a seller when selling is the bottleneck.

That tells you the plan.
It does not tell you the result.

The company did share one number. It needs a closer look.

More than 100 enterprises and government institutions are building on its platform, the company said.
That is company-reported. “𝗕𝘂𝗶𝗹𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗼𝗻” 𝗶𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 “𝗽𝗮𝘆𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗳𝗼𝗿.”

Here is what the report leaves out:

No revenue figure.
No count of paying customers.
No contract lengths.
No pricing.

Think of a famous coach joining a team.
It says the club wants to win more.
It does not say the team is winning.

That’s not a knock on Sarvam. Selling to large organizations is hard, and hiring someone who has done it is sensible.
𝗜𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝘀𝗼𝗻𝗮𝗯𝗹𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝘁. 𝗜𝘁 𝗶𝘀 𝘀𝘁𝗶𝗹𝗹 𝗮 𝗯𝗲𝘁.

𝗔 𝗳𝗮𝗺𝗼𝘂𝘀 𝗵𝗶𝗿𝗲 𝗮𝗻𝗻𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗰𝗲𝘀 𝗮 𝗽𝗹𝗮𝗻. 𝗜𝘁 𝗱𝗼𝗲𝘀 𝗻𝗼𝘁 𝗽𝗿𝗼𝘃𝗲 𝗮 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁.

The useful test: what shows up next that a hire cannot fake?
A first revenue figure.
A named large contract.

Agree or disagree, and why: a famous hire shows where a startup is stuck, not that it is winning.

Source: Business Standard, Nov 9, 2026.

Your next great hire is asking ChatGPT what your team really think of you
And why that’s good news for decent employers:

New data from Indeed, reported by Kristin Stoller at Fortune: 

~70% of job seekers now use AI tools to research employers.

And when those tools answer questions about company culture, around 40% of what they cite comes from Glassdoor and Indeed, rather than the company careers page.

A few years ago, a company’s real culture only revealed itself once you’d signed the contract.

Now it’s on the record, and you’re being compared side by side with everyone else.

That’s a challenge, but it’s also a rare opportunity for genuinely good employers to show what they do, why they do it and why new talent should choose them.

AI learns from what’s written down, so think about where your employer brand lives in words:

→ Review sites and forums: Glassdoor, Indeed, Reddit threads

→ Your website: Interview your team, ask clients what it’s like to work with you, spotlight career journeys, training opps and what people have learned

→ And the obvious one… your employees’ LinkedIn

LinkedIn is already one of the most-cited sources in AI search (in 11% of answers - Semrush), but on ‘what’s it like to work here’ questions it’s only around 4%. To me, that’s a big opportunity: AI already trusts LinkedIn and presents the perfect gap for your team to fill.

Imagine a potential new hire researching you and being pointed straight to a colleague’s post about their promotion, a project they loved or what they’ve learned this year.

It doesn’t need to be polished or formal - it’s the candid, human bits that often tip someone towards you. 

Hiring is hard. If you can’t pay the highest salary or offer the biggest benefits package, this is one way you can punch well above your weight. More than ever, people want to work for companies that share their values, doing work they actually enjoy.  

Your 5-min task for today: an AI audit. 

Ask Claude/ChatGPT what it’s like to work at your company. 
(Use a logged-out or incognito chat, so it isn’t drawing on what it already knows about you) 

Would love to know what, if anything, it came back with!

AI is an investment. “Faster” is not a business case!

I’m getting more and more questions about how to use AI effectively in HR, and yes - AI can be a powerful accelerator. But in practice, I still see considerable time, budget, and management attention going into tools and use cases before the underlying question is clear:

What business outcome are we investing in, and what is currently preventing it?


Let’s make this concrete with a recruitment example:

A company struggles to fill business-critical roles. Vacancies put pressure on existing teams and delay planned growth. The proposed solution: AI-assisted screening to identify suitable candidates faster.

A reasonable idea. But before investing, look at what happens between receiving an application and signing a contract. Imagine that analysis reveals the following:

Recruiters already identify suitable candidates promptly. Those candidates then wait for interview feedback. Hiring managers revisit requirements mid-process. Final offers stall because approval responsibilities are unclear. AI could shorten screening.
It would leave those delays largely untouched.

The investment might reduce recruiting effort. But the business case was about filling critical roles sooner, and enabling the business to deliver.

Those are different benefits! We need to distinguish them.

In this example, clearer requirements, agreed decision timelines, and explicit approval responsibilities would address the sources of delay. AI could then be assessed against the remaining constraints.

This is why HR process analysis is central to my work on value creation: it connects the business objective with operational reality -where work waits, where decisions stall, where rework occurs, and what those conditions mean for performance. 

That evidence helps us decide what to change, where AI can contribute, and how to test whether the benefit justifies the full investment. For recruitment, that means measuring more than screening speed: time to fill critical roles, hiring quality, and total human effort, including review and correction.

Before asking, “Where can we use AI?”, I want to answer:

If we invest here, what will improve for the business, and why?

Save this five-question checklist for your next discussion about AI-HR investments, and feel free to reach out to me if you need a critical perspective.

Thank you, David Green 🇺🇦, your October newsletter on the redesign of work ties directly into this: Understanding how work actually happens is crucial for determining where AI can add value.

One AI tool can now predict 95% of what evaluators will criticise (its vendor says). 
It means better proposals are coming. Not better projects.

The 95% figure comes from the vendor’s own test, about 25 Horizon Europe proposals, with its report compared to the official evaluation reports.
Another tool promises an estimated score per evaluation criterion before you submit.

I do not think these tools are wrong.
On the contrary: I am afraid they are right.

Several proposal writing and testing tools are trained on past proposals and evaluation reports.
So they have learned what scores well:
Clear objectives. Strong impact language. A tidy work plan.

What they cannot see is what I hear from people who run these projects after the contract:
→ staff costs planned before anyone knew who would do the work
→ the first deliverable due in month six, while hiring takes five months
→ co-financing confirmed in the proposal, but missing from the partner’s own budget

None of this loses points at evaluation, because the text reads well.
But it shows in year one, when the money is already committed.

A tool can tell you how the evaluator will read your proposal.
It cannot tell you whether your partners can do the work.

On Thursday, in our last roundtable of 2026, we follow these projects after they are funded.

I have a feeling the LinkedIn algorithm isn’t going to like this one. 😅

Last week I had coffee with a couple of founder friends. Both are close to securing their first round, and neither has hired at any real scale before. When we got onto hiring, the plan was one I hear a lot: “First thing, we’ll get LinkedIn Recruiter and some job slots.”

I call it plug-and-play hiring. Get the seat and the slots, message your network, then call a trusted recruiter at 20–30% of salary per hire.

Completely understandable. But a Recruiter seat alone is estimated at around $9–12k a year (yes, Recruiter Lite is cheaper, but it’s restricted). Add a few agency fees and a decent chunk of your round has gone before anyone’s started.

So I shared what I’ve seen work.

Most startups already use Notion or Confluence, so put your culture and open roles on a simple page there. It costs nothing and says more than a job ad.

For sourcing, AI tools like Juicebox and Metaview now do a lot of the heavy lifting. Both have free plans to try, and paid ones start from around $60–120 a month per seat. That’s a fraction of a Recruiter licence.

And rather than paying a recruiter/agency per hire, bring one in for the hiring push, either embedded or on contract. They run the process, build your pipeline, and when they leave, you’ve got a system you can run yourselves.

I’m not anti-LinkedIn. I’m posting this on here, after all. I just don’t think it should be your default starting point.

#Startups #Hiring #TalentAcquisition #Founders #Scaling

If you’ve spent much time on LinkedIn this year, you’ll have seen the posts. Someone builds a whole product with AI over a coffee and croissant, with no developers and no team.

I don’t think the people posting them are lying, exactly. The bit you can show on screen really can come together exceptionally fast but it’s everything underneath it that tends not to make the video.

This week’s guest on The Frontier Leader Show got his front end live in a weekend but he’s refreshingly honest about what it took to build the rest afterwards.

Tony D’Agostino spent 24 years in the US Navy. He started as a rescue swimmer jumping out of helicopters and finished driving aircraft carriers. Then the man who hired him onto Wall Street told him that anyone who could run a carrier could help run a trading desk. He was right, and a presidential nomination to the SIPC board came later.

What stuck with me was how he described each of those moves. He’d take something as far as he could on his own, then bring in people who knew more than he did. SpeakerAgent.ai got built exactly the same way.

A few other things from the conversation:
✳️ One podcast appearance that turned into a contract within a fortnight. 
✳️ Who he thinks ends up calling the shots once AI is writing most of the code
✳️ What a sports coach knows about hiring that a lot of org charts forget
✳️ The decision he’d reverse if he started again. Nothing to do with which AI tool he picked.

Thanks to Tony D'Agostino for a generous and very honest hour. If you’re an expert who’d rather be speaking than pitching, SpeakerAgent.ai is worth a look.
